clinicalPearls: Autosomal recessive urea cycle disorder caused by defective mitochondrial ornithine transporter (ORNT1, encoded by SLC25A15), which impairs ornithine entry into mitochondria.
Defined by the biochemical triad of hyperornithinaemia, episodic hyperammonaemia and homocitrullinuria, hence the name.

Presentation is highly variable: neonatal hyperammonaemic crises at one extreme, and at the other a chronic neurological phenotype with progressive spastic paraparesis, ataxia and learning difficulties.
Protein aversion, recurrent vomiting and episodic encephalopathy triggered by protein load or catabolism are common; some patients have coagulopathy and raised liver enzymes.

Cytosolic ornithine accumulates while mitochondrial ornithine is deficient, so the urea cycle stalls and excess carbamoyl phosphate reacts with lysine to form homocitrulline and is diverted to orotic acid.
Acute hyperammonaemia is managed with protein withdrawal, high-energy intake to reverse catabolism, nitrogen scavengers and arginine or citrulline, with dialysis for severe elevation.

Long-term treatment is a protein-restricted diet with citrulline or arginine supplementation; unlike some other urea cycle disorders, ornithine supplementation is not used because transport into mitochondria is the defect.
The chronic spastic paraparesis can mimic hereditary spastic paraplegia, so biochemical screening is warranted in unexplained progressive spasticity with cognitive involvement.
reference.pathophysiology: The urea cycle spans both the mitochondrial matrix and the cytosol, and ornithine must be shuttled into mitochondria to accept the carbamoyl group and regenerate citrulline. HHH syndrome results from loss of function of the inner mitochondrial membrane ornithine/citrulline antiporter ORNT1. Ornithine is therefore trapped in the cytosol, producing hyperornithinaemia, while its deficiency within mitochondria limits ornithine transcarbamylase activity and stalls ureagenesis, causing episodic hyperammonaemia. The carbamoyl phosphate that cannot be consumed accumulates and reacts non-enzymatically with lysine to yield homocitrulline, which appears in the urine, and is also diverted into the pyrimidine pathway to generate orotic acid. The neurological features, including the characteristic slowly progressive pyramidal and cerebellar dysfunction, are thought to reflect the combined effects of intermittent hyperammonaemia, disturbed intracellular ornithine and creatine metabolism, and possibly the effects of accumulated metabolites on the central nervous system. A partially functional back-up ornithine transporter (ORNT2) may account for the milder and variable phenotype compared with a complete urea cycle block, and residual transporter activity influences severity.
additionalDifferentials: Other urea cycle disorders (ornithine transcarbamylase deficiency, citrullinaemia, argininosuccinic aciduria)
Gyrate atrophy from ornithine aminotransferase deficiency (also hyperornithinaemia but distinct clinical picture)
Hereditary spastic paraplegia (for the chronic neurological phenotype)
additionalInvestigations: Plasma amino acids demonstrating hyperornithinaemia with variable citrulline
Urine amino acids and orotic acid showing homocitrullinuria and orotic aciduria
Molecular genetic testing of the SLC25A15 gene
Liver function tests and coagulation profile
Neuroimaging and nerve conduction or evoked potential studies in the chronic neurological phenotype
Assessment of protein tolerance and dietary protein intake history
redFlags: Acute hyperammonaemic encephalopathy with declining consciousness
Progressive lower limb spasticity with cognitive decline
Coagulopathy or acute liver dysfunction during metabolic decompensation
Seizures or signs of raised intracranial pressure during a crisis
reference.prognosis: Prognosis is variable and depends on presentation and how well hyperammonaemia is controlled; early recognition and consistent dietary and pharmacological management can prevent crises, but chronic neurological impairment such as spastic paraparesis may progress despite good metabolic control.
pitfalls: Giving ornithine supplementation, which is ineffective because the defect is impaired mitochondrial ornithine transport
Mistaking the chronic spastic phenotype for hereditary spastic paraplegia and missing the metabolic cause
Overlooking the diagnosis when hyperammonaemia is only intermittent and normal between episodes
Failing to recognise coagulopathy and hepatic dysfunction as part of the disorder
Under-treating catabolic stress, allowing recurrent hyperammonaemic decompensation
references: Standard textbook of inborn errors of metabolism
International urea cycle disorder management guidelines
management: Long-term management centres on a protein-restricted diet with essential amino acid supplementation and citrulline or arginine supplementation to sustain ureagenesis
Add nitrogen-scavenging therapy such as sodium benzoate or sodium phenylbutyrate to enhance alternative nitrogen excretion

Treat acute hyperammonaemic crises by stopping protein intake, delivering high-energy intravenous glucose and lipid to reverse catabolism, giving intravenous nitrogen scavengers and arginine, and instituting haemodialysis for severe hyperammonaemia
Avoid catabolic triggers and use an emergency sick-day regimen with increased energy intake during intercurrent illness, fasting or surgery
Monitor plasma ammonia and amino acids, growth, liver function, coagulation and neurological status over time
Coordinate care with a specialist metabolic team and metabolic dietitian, and escalate urgently for encephalopathy or vomiting suggesting decompensation
Offer genetic counselling and family testing given autosomal recessive inheritance of SLC25A15 variants
